query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled annealing of the as-solidified, non‐equilibrium Mg‐containing lightweight HEA drives a phase evolution in which the initially dispersed, metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases transform into more stable, continuous phases that promote the formation of a protective external oxide film. This film, enriched in Mg-derived oxides (and possibly coupled with other oxide formers in the alloy), leads to enhanced high‐temperature oxidation resistance and lower corrosion rates relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (density below 6 g/cm³) comprising a mixture of metastable solid solution regions and discrete Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: A systematic post-processing thermal treatment (controlled annealing at specified temperatures and durations) to induce a stepwise transformation of metastable phases.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under identical baseline chemical compositions and density constraints; evaluated both in corrosive environments (e.g., immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) and under high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution and connectivity of Mg-rich intermetallic phases, which upon annealing coalesce into stable, continuous phases that assist in the formation of a coherent and adherent oxide scale (rich in MgO and, if present, supplemented by other protective oxides from alloy constituents).
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment promotes the transformation of scattered, metastable Mg-rich phases into a more uniform, stable phase distribution. This rearrangement drives the segregation of Mg to the surface or grain boundaries during subsequent exposure, catalyzing the growth of a continuous, protective oxide film that reduces both the corrosion kinetics and high-temperature oxidation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-solidified baseline alloy, the annealed samples will exhibit a more continuous and adherent oxide scale, lower corrosion rates in NaCl solutions, and reduced oxidation weight gain during high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The non-equilibrium, rapidly cooled HEA with discrete, metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases that yield less continuous or protective oxide films under aggressive service conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under the density constraint (<6 g/cm³) and within the tested environmental conditions (i.e., room temperature corrosion in salt solutions and high-temperature oxidation tests). The effect is expected to hold provided the alloy composition and processing windows are maintained within the studied range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact annealing parameters (temperature and time) necessary to achieve the optimum phase transformation and the precise characteristics of the protective oxide film (e.g., phase composition, thickness) are not yet quantified. It is also uncertain how minor compositional variations may affect the transformation kinetics and the resulting corrosion/oxidation performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples (with overall density <6 g/cm³). Retain one set in the as-solidified (rapidly cooled) state and subject the other set to controlled annealing treatments (varying temperature and duration). Expose both sets to identical corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) and high-temperature oxidation tests. Characterize the microstructures (using XRD, TEM) and the surface oxide scales (using SEM, XPS) as well as measure corrosion rates and oxidation weight gain.
measurements: Phase identification and distribution via XRD and TEM
Surface oxide film continuity and composition via SEM and XPS
Corrosion rates measured by electrochemical techniques (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization)
Oxidation kinetics measured by periodic weight gain at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxide film continuity (i.e., protective scale formation) and do not show reduced corrosion rates and oxidation weight gain relative to the as-solidified baseline samples, then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .

By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

decision.trend: Early investigations into non‐equilibrium lightweight and high‐entropy alloys (including the Al–Mg‐rich systems) established that rapid processing yields structurally complex microstructures – a mix of metastable solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Over time, researchers shifted attention from merely quantifying mechanical properties (such as hardness and room‐temperature compression) toward beginning to probe how these metastable states evolve when subjected to more aggressive conditions. The most recent studies have started to correlate phase‐transformation phenomena during thermal or environmental exposures with subsequent changes in high‐temperature oxidation and corrosion behavior, although they have not yet directly linked the transformation pathways with the functional performance of alloys containing reactive species such as Mg.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved how the inherent non‐equilibrium microstructure featuring metastable intermetallic compounds transforms during subsequent exposure (e.g., under high-temperature oxidation and corrosive environments) and exactly how the evolution in phase connectivity—especially with Mg’s strong propensity to segregate and modify local chemistry—affects the surface passivation and overall corrosion kinetics. There is a need for a controlled study that decouples the influence of processing‐induced metastability from the ensuing phase evolution and its impact on corrosion and oxidation behavior under identical baseline composition and density constraints.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the post-processing thermal treatment (e.g., controlled annealing temperature and duration) on a baseline non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA to induce a stepwise transformation from metastable intermetallics to more stable phases
decision.why: This approach follows the emerging trend of moving from simple mechanical testing towards understanding transformation kinetics that dictate functional behavior. By comparing samples maintained in the rapid‐cooled metastable state (baseline) with those subjected to systematically varied annealing treatments, one can directly correlate changes in microstructural evolution—such as the refinement or coalescence of Mg-rich intermetallic phases—with measurable changes in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation performance. If, for instance, the annealed samples develop a more continuous and protective oxide film and show reduced corrosion rates relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is supported; the absence of such differences would falsify it.
